positions.A: The allegations of rape and sexual misconduct against Eric Swalwell are credible and warranted his resignation from Congress and suspension of his gubernatorial campaign.
positions.B: The allegations against Eric Swalwell are unproven and possibly politically motivated, and he should be presumed innocent pending the outcome of criminal investigations.

title: Kurds in Lebanon
neutral_summary: Kurds in Lebanon are people born in or residing in Lebanon who are of full or partial Kurdish origin. Estimates on the number of Kurds in Lebanon prior to 1985 were around 60,000. Today, there are tens of thousands of Kurds in Lebanon, mainly in Beirut.

positions.A: Kurds in Lebanon face systemic barriers to citizenship and civil rights that leave many stateless or marginalized despite long-term residence.
positions.B: The Lebanese state's citizenship and residency policies toward Kurds are a legitimate exercise of national sovereignty and administrative order, not discriminatory targeting.

title: Battle of Anandpur (1700)
neutral_summary: The Battle of Anandpur was fought at Anandpur, between the armies of the Sikh Guru Gobind Singh and the Mughal forces aided by the Nawab of Bahawalpur state, Rajas of the Sivalik Hills.

positions.A: The Mughal forces and their allied Hill Rajas were justified in attacking Anandpur to curb the growing military and political power of Guru Gobind Singh, which they saw as a threat to regional order and imperial authority.
positions.B: Guru Gobind Singh's forces were justified in defending Anandpur against an unprovoked assault by Mughal-aligned rulers seeking to suppress Sikh autonomy and religious freedom.

title: Battle of Delhi (1764)
neutral_summary: The Battle of Delhi (1764) was fought between the ruler of Kingdom of Bharatpur and the Rohilkhand Kingdom. Jawahar Singh of Bharatpur invaded and plundered Delhi with the military support of the Marathas of Holkar dynasty and Sikh cavalry. However failed to yield any success.

positions.A: The Battle of Delhi (1764) was a strategic invasion by Jawahar Singh of Bharatpur to assert dominance over Delhi with the support of Maratha and Sikh allies.
positions.B: The Battle of Delhi (1764) was an unsuccessful plundering raid by Jawahar Singh that failed to achieve any lasting territorial or political gain.

title: Battle of Anandpur (1699)
neutral_summary: The Battle of Anandpur was fought between the Sikh forces led by Guru Gobind Singh and the Hill State forces by Alim and Balia Chand. This was the first major battle fought after the formation of the Khalsa.

positions.A: The Battle of Anandpur was a defensive engagement in which the newly formed Khalsa under Guru Gobind Singh legitimately resisted aggression from the Hill State forces.
positions.B: The Battle of Anandpur was a conflict provoked by the growing military assertiveness of the Khalsa, which threatened the traditional authority of the Hill State rulers led by Alim Chand and Balia Chand.

title: Battle of Anandpur (1685)
neutral_summary: The Battle of Anandpur (1685) was fought between the Sikhs and an allied force of rajas of the Hill States of the Sivalik range, specifically Kahlur, Kangra, and Guler.

positions.A: The battle was provoked by the Hill State rajas' aggression against Guru Gobind Singh and the growing Sikh community at Anandpur.
positions.B: The battle resulted from Sikh expansionism and assertiveness that threatened the traditional authority of the Hill State rajas.

title: Battle of Anandpur (1682)
neutral_summary: The Battle of Anandpur was fought by the Sikh forces led by Guru Gobind Singh and the Kahlur forces led by Bhim Chand. This was also the first battle fought by Guru Gobind Singh.

positions.A: The battle was provoked by Raja Bhim Chand's hostility and demands for tribute, forcing Guru Gobind Singh's Sikh forces into a defensive war to protect Anandpur.
positions.B: The battle arose because Guru Gobind Singh's growing military power and refusal to submit to Kahlur's traditional authority threatened Bhim Chand's sovereignty, justifying his armed response.

title: First Battle of Anandpur (1704)
neutral_summary: The First Battle of Anandpur in 1704 was fought between the Mughal Empire and the Sikhs.

positions.A: The Mughal forces successfully besieged Anandpur and forced the Sikhs under Guru Gobind Singh to abandon the fort through military pressure and blockade.
positions.B: The Sikh defenders under Guru Gobind Singh withstood the Mughal siege and only left Anandpur later under a negotiated safe-passage agreement rather than due to being militarily defeated.

title: Second siege of Anandpur
neutral_summary: The second siege of Anandpur (anadapura dī ghērābadī), also known as the second battle of Anandpur (1704)  (anadapura dī dūjī laṛā'ī sāla satārāṁ sau cāra), was a siege at Anandpur, between Sikhs and the Mughal governors, dispatched by Aurangzeb, Wazir Khan, Dilwaar Kahn and Zaberdast Khan, and aided by the vassal Rajas of the Sivalik Hills which lasted from May 1704 to 19 December 1704.

positions.A: The Mughal commanders and hill Rajas treacherously violated their sworn oath of safe passage, attacking the Sikhs after they evacuated Anandpur.
positions.B: The Mughal and allied forces were conducting a legitimate military campaign to subdue a fortified rebel stronghold and did not breach any binding agreement.

title: Security Zone (Lebanon)
neutral_summary:
Israeli Security Zone may refer to:

Israeli occupation of Southern Lebanon (2026), "Security Zone" as part of the 2026 Lebanon war
The Israeli occupation of Southern Lebanon (1982–2000) following the creation of the Free Lebanon State
Philadelphi Route, a narrow strip of land between Gaza Strip and Egypt
The Gaza envelope
The Seam zone

positions.A: Israel's establishment of security zones in Southern Lebanon and around Gaza is a necessary defensive measure to protect Israeli territory from cross-border attacks.
positions.B: Israel's establishment of security zones in Southern Lebanon and around Gaza constitutes an illegal occupation that violates the sovereignty and rights of Lebanese and Palestinian populations.

title: Ziaul Ahsan
neutral_summary: Ziaul Ahsan (born 4 December 1970) is a former two-star officer of the Bangladesh Army and the antecedent director general of the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre. Ahsan is known for his alleged extrajudicial and enforced disappearance assignments while tenuring at Rapid Action Battalion under the regime of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. He was relieved of his duties and detained forthwith after the Student–People's uprising. The Daily Amar Desh and Mohammad Tajul Islam alleged that he killed a total of 1,030 enforced disappeared persons during his career at the order of Sheikh Hasina.

positions.A: Ziaul Ahsan orchestrated extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances of over a thousand people while at the Rapid Action Battalion under orders from Sheikh Hasina's government.
positions.B: The allegations against Ziaul Ahsan are politically motivated accusations by opponents of the former Hasina government and lack sufficient proof of his direct culpability.

title: Misinformation about violence by transgender people
neutral_summary:
In the 2020s, right-wing politicians and commentators have falsely claimed that transgender people commit disproportionately higher rates of violence, such as mass shootings or terrorist attacks. Various hoaxes have also misidentified perpetrators of violent incidents as transgender. This misinformation is primarily generated and circulated within the United States, particularly on social media. It has been amplified by Trumpist voices such as Donald Trump Jr., Libs of TikTok owner Chaya Raichik, and The Heritage Foundation, and has spread internationally through foreign outlets and figures, including RT in Russia.
Members of the second Trump administration have suggested policies on the basis of these claims, including for the Department of Justice to revoke trans people's right to possess firearms. The Heritage Foundation petitioned the FBI to designate "Transgender Ideology-Inspired Violent Extremism" as a domestic terrorism threat category. As of February 2026, neither policy has been enacted. Following the assassination of Charlie Kirk, Texas US representative Ronny Jackson called for trans people to be taken "off the streets".
According to Ohio State University professor of human security Laura Dugan, the threat of transgender shooters is "just not a concern," and transgender people are underrepresented as perpetrators of mass shootings. Analyses of the topic have noted that transgender people are substantially more likely to be victims than the perpetrators of violence. According to subject-matter experts, disinformation casting transgender people as violent is used to legitimize anti-trans violence and legislation, particularly as part of a broader anti-LGBTQ backlash in the United States.

positions.A: Transgender people are disproportionately likely to commit mass shootings and violent attacks, justifying policies like firearm restrictions and domestic terrorism classifications targeting them.
positions.B: Claims that transgender people are disproportionately violent are misinformation, as data show trans people are far more often victims than perpetrators of violence, and such claims are used to justify anti-trans discrimination and legislation.

title: Battle of Basarke
neutral_summary: The Battle of Basarke, also known as Battle of Basarke and Hujra Shah was fought on 23 October 1736 between the Sikh forces led by Nawab Kapur Singh and the Mughal forces led by Lakhpat Rai.

positions.A: The Sikh forces under Nawab Kapur Singh achieved a significant victory that demonstrated their growing military strength against Mughal authority.
positions.B: The Mughal forces under Lakhpat Rai were defending legitimate imperial control of the region against a Sikh insurgency.

title: Syrian Social Nationalist Party in Lebanon
neutral_summary:
The Syrian Social Nationalist Party in Lebanon (SSNP-L) is a Syrian nationalist party operating in Lebanon. The Lebanese section of the Syrian Social Nationalist Party advocates subsuming Lebanon into a Greater Syrian nation state spanning the Fertile Crescent.
Founded in Beirut in 1932 as a national liberation organization hostile to French colonialism, the party played a significant role in Lebanese politics and was involved in attempted coup d'etats in 1949 and 1961 following which it was thoroughly repressed. It was active in the Lebanese Civil War, particularly in clashes with the right-wing  Lebanese Front, resistance against the Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 1982 and in the South Lebanon conflict from 1985 to 2000 while also continuously supporting the Syrian occupation in Lebanon.

positions.A: Lebanon should be unified with Syria and the wider Fertile Crescent into a single Greater Syrian nation, dissolving Lebanon's separate political identity.
positions.B: Lebanon should remain a distinct, sovereign nation-state with its own identity, separate from Syria and any Greater Syrian political union.

title: Hezbollah political activities
neutral_summary:
Along with the Amal Movement, Hezbollah is one of the two main parties representing the Shia community, Lebanon's largest religious bloc. Amal has made a commitment to carrying out its activities through political means, but remains a partial fighting force aiding Hezbollah when the need arises.
Hezbollah has been a part of Lebanese governments since November 2005.

positions.A: Hezbollah's participation in Lebanese government since 2005 represents legitimate political representation of the Shia community and democratic integration.
positions.B: Hezbollah's political participation is illegitimate because it uses its armed militia to coerce Lebanese politics, undermining state sovereignty and democratic governance.

title: Funding of Hezbollah
neutral_summary:
The funding of Hezbollah comes from Lebanese business groups, private persons, businessmen, the Lebanese diaspora involved in African diamond exploration, other Islamic groups and countries, and the taxes paid by the Shia Lebanese. Hezbollah says that the main source of its income comes from its own investment portfolios and donations by Muslims.
Western sources maintain that Hezbollah receives most of its financial, training, weapons, explosives, political, diplomatic, and organizational aid from the Islamic Republic of Iran and Ba'athist Syria. Iran is said to have given $400 million between 1983 and 1989 through donation. The situation changed due to economic problems, but in 2013 Iran still funded humanitarian efforts carried on by Hezbollah. According to reports released in February 2010, Hezbollah received $400 million from Iran. In 2011, Iran earmarked $7 million to Hezbollah's activities in Latin America. Hezbollah also receives financial and political assistance, as well as weapons and training, from Iran. Iranian support to Hezbollah has varied over the years, but as of 2018 US officials estimate Iran transfers $700 million annually.
Hezbollah has relied also on funding from the Shi'ite Lebanese Diaspora in West Africa, the United States and, most importantly, the Triple Frontier, or tri-border area, along the junction of Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay. U.S. law enforcement officials have identified an illegal multimillion-dollar cigarette-smuggling fund raising operation and a drug smuggling operation. However, Nasrallah has repeatedly denied any links between the South American drug trade and Hezbollah, calling such accusations "propaganda" and attempts "to damage the image of Hezbollah".

positions.A: Hezbollah's funding derives primarily from Iranian and Syrian state sponsorship, including major cash transfers for weapons, training, and operations.
positions.B: Hezbollah's funding derives mainly from its own legitimate investments, business networks, and voluntary donations from Muslims and the Lebanese diaspora, not foreign state patronage or illicit activity.

title: Lavash
neutral_summary:
Lavash is a thin flatbread made of leavened or unleavened wheat dough, baked in a tandoor (a type of clay oven) or on a saj griddle. Some forms are sourdough fermented with dough from previous batches. Lavash cooks very quickly in a tandoor, being placed on the sides using a cushion. It is large and thin, though there are many variations in size and shape. It is soft when fresh but is often dried. Lavash is common to the cuisines of South Caucasus and West Asia. It is a staple food in Armenia, eastern Georgia, and parts of Iran.
Soft lavash can be used for wraps, which use ingredients such as kebabs, barbecued meat, or cheese. It may also be served with dip or with stew to be eaten by hand. Lavash is often prepared in large batches. It lasts months once dried and can be hydrated to restore softness. Dried lavash is sometimes broken up and eaten in dishes such as the Armenian stew khash.
Lavash originated in ancient times, with several countries claiming its origin. In the modern day, lavash is widespread in many parts of Asia between Turkey and Kashmir, and also exists in other regions where it was introduced by Armenian immigrants. It is served at many restaurants, as well as at weddings. In Armenian culture, the preparation of lavash by women is a community event. The UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List inscribed lavash "as an expression of culture in Armenia" in 2014. This was controversial in other countries in the region, and a separate listing regarding the culture of lavash and other flatbreads in Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkey was inscribed in 2016.

positions.A: Lavash is a distinctly Armenian culinary tradition, justifying its inscription on the UNESCO list as an expression of Armenian culture.
positions.B: Lavash is a shared regional flatbread tradition across the South Caucasus and West Asia, so singling it out as uniquely Armenian heritage is inaccurate and unfair to other countries.

title: Naval Support Activity Bahrain
neutral_summary:
Naval Support Activity Bahrain (or NSA Bahrain) is a United States Navy base situated in the Kingdom of Bahrain and is home to U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and United States Fifth Fleet.
Occupying the original territory of the British Royal Navy base known as HMS Jufair, U.S. Navy presence was established on-site during World War II. Transferred to the U.S. government in 1971, NSA Bahrain provides support through logistical, supply, and protection as well as a Navy Exchange facility and Morale, Welfare and Recreation programs to United States Armed Forces and coalition assets. 
The commander of Navy Region Europe, Africa, Southwest Asia is responsible for NSA Bahrain and Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. Navy Region Europe, Africa, Southwest Asia is responsible to Navy Installations Command, though it has close coordination with Naval Forces Central Command.

positions.A: NSA Bahrain is a vital strategic asset that ensures regional stability and protects U.S. and allied interests in the Persian Gulf.
positions.B: NSA Bahrain represents an entrenchment of U.S. military power that props up an authoritarian monarchy and entangles the U.S. in regional conflicts.

title: Hananya Naftali
neutral_summary: Hananya Naftali (Hebrew: חנניה נפתלי; born 7 July 1995) is an Israeli journalist and YouTuber. He served as a digital aide to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

positions.A: Hananya Naftali is a legitimate journalist and effective digital advocate who presents Israel's perspective to a global audience.
positions.B: Hananya Naftali is a Netanyahu-aligned propagandist whose content spreads biased or misleading narratives rather than objective journalism.

title: Laxmipeta Massacre
neutral_summary:
Laxmipeta Massacre refers to a brutal caste-based attack that occurred in Laxmipeta village, Vangara mandal, Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, on June 12, 2012. The violence was initiated by members of the Kapu caste against the landless Mala (Dalit) community, resulting in the deaths of five Dalits and injuries to several others. The assailants, armed with sticks, axes, spears, and country-made bombs, launched an unprovoked assault on the Dalit colony, causing significant damage and displacing many residents.
The Kapus, who held economic power and growing political influence in the region, were reportedly unwilling to acknowledge the Dalits' traditional claims to land. The incident was a culmination of escalating tensions and systematic violence, triggered by the Dalits' assertion of their rights and their resistance against perceived oppression. This massacre highlighted the persistent discriminatory and violent tendencies of caste hierarchies in modern Indian society, drawing widespread condemnation from Dalit activists and human rights organisations. Following the incident, the Crime Investigation Department (CID) identified approximately 80 Kapus for their role in the violence, and later a significant number of Kapu accused were subsequently arrested and jailed, demonstrating the scale and magnitude of the attack. It also generated widespread outrage from Dalit activists of the state and led to the formation of Andhra Pradesh Dalit Mahasabha which drew inspiration from Ambedkar's ideals and stood for Dalit rights, and fought against untouchability and exclusion.

positions.A: The Laxmipeta attack was a caste-motivated massacre by dominant Kapu caste members seeking to suppress Dalit land rights claims and assert social dominance.
positions.B: The Laxmipeta incident stemmed from a land dispute between two communities that escalated into mutual violence, rather than being a premeditated caste-based massacre.

title: Kandra (caste)
neutral_summary: Kandra, also known as Kandara or Kodama is a Scheduled Caste community in East India, primarily in Odisha and West Bengal. They were traditionally engaged in the profession of fishing and artisan, though in the modern times many of the members of community have integrated in society.

positions.A: The Kandra community's classification as a Scheduled Caste is justified given their historically marginalized socio-economic status.
positions.B: The Kandra community's Scheduled Caste classification is outdated or overly broad, as many members have since integrated into mainstream society and no longer face the same disadvantages.

title: Mughal–Safavid war (1649–1653)
neutral_summary: The Mughal–Safavid war of 1649–1653 was fought between the Mughal and Safavid empires in the territory of modern Afghanistan. While the Mughals were at war with the Janid Uzbeks, the Safavid army captured the fortress city of Kandahar and other strategic cities that controlled the region. The Mughals attempted to regain the city, but their efforts were proven unsuccessful.

positions.A: Kandahar and its surrounding region were rightfully Safavid territory, justifying their capture while the Mughals were distracted by war with the Janid Uzbeks.
positions.B: Kandahar was legitimately Mughal territory, and the Safavid seizure of it constituted an unlawful act of opportunistic aggression.

title: Mughal conquest of Kashmir
neutral_summary: The Mughal conquest of Kashmir was an invasion of the Kashmir Sultanate by the Mughal Empire in 1585–1589. After severe fighting and heavy casualties, the Mughals defeated the Kashmiris in the Battle of Hastivanj (10 October 1586).

positions.A: The Mughal conquest of Kashmir was a legitimate imperial expansion that brought the region under a more stable, unified administration.
positions.B: The Mughal conquest of Kashmir was an unjust invasion that violently ended Kashmiri sovereignty and independence.

title: Destruction of the Rafi'-Nia synagogue
neutral_summary: On 7 April 2026, during the 2026 Iran war, the Rafi'-Nia synagogue in Tehran was completely destroyed during an Israeli Air Force strike on an adjacent building. The incident was condemned by Iranian authorities and the local Jewish community. The Israel Defense Force (IDF) said it "regrets" the destruction of the synagogue.

positions.A: The destruction of the Rafi'-Nia synagogue was an unintended and regrettable consequence of a legitimate Israeli military strike on an adjacent target, not a deliberate act against the Jewish community.
positions.B: The destruction of the Rafi'-Nia synagogue reflects reckless disregard by Israeli forces for civilian and religious sites, making the strike unjustifiable regardless of intent.

title: Bodinayakkanur
neutral_summary:
Bodinayakanur is a town in the state of Tamil Nadu, India. Nestled at the base of the Western Ghat Hills, the town is widely known as India's cardamom capital for its pedigree in cultivating that crop.
Despite a population estimated to be no higher than 0.2% of Tamilnadu's total population, Bodinayakanur has been the constituency for 2 of 12 Chief Ministers of the state.

positions.A: Bodinayakkanur's disproportionate production of Chief Ministers reflects genuine political influence and leadership talent nurtured in the region.
positions.B: Bodinayakkanur's outsized share of Chief Ministers despite its small population points to entrenched local political dynasties and patronage networks rather than broad-based merit.

title: Zamindars of Bihar
neutral_summary:
The Zamindars of Bihar were the autonomous rulers and administrators of the Bihar Subah during Mughal rule and later during British rule. They formed the landed aristocracy that lasted until Indian independence in 1947. The zamindars of Bihar were numerous and could be divided into small, medium and large depending on how much land they controlled. Within Bihar, the zamindars had both economic and military power. Each zamindari would have its own standing army which was typically composed of the zamindar's own clansmen.
The majority of these zamindars usually belonged to Hindu communities such as Bhumihars, Rajputs, Brahmins, Kayasthas or Muslims.

positions.A: The Zamindars of Bihar functioned as a legitimate landed aristocracy that provided administrative and military stability under Mughal and British rule.
positions.B: The Zamindars of Bihar represented an exploitative feudal system that entrenched caste-based land monopolies and oppressed peasant cultivators.

title: List of active Indian Navy ships
neutral_summary:
The Indian Navy, the naval warfare branch of the Indian Armed Forces, operated a fleet of about 145 surface combatant vessels and submarines as of November 2025. By inventory, the Indian Navy's principal assets include its aircraft carriers – the service has operated four aircraft carriers since 1961, and submarines – which presently includes a strategic submarine force. It also operates a fleet of amphibious assault ships, guided missile destroyers, and stealth frigates amongst others. However, it still lacks certain capability-specific assets such as mine countermeasures vessels, and has quantitatively inadequate fleet of certain vessels such as attack submarines.
The Indian Naval fleet inventory is divided amongst its three regional formations:

Western Naval Command: Headquartered in Mumbai, it consists of the Western Fleet – responsible for naval operations in the Arabian Sea, which flanks India's western coastline. Given its geographical location, it is central to any conflict involving Pakistan.
Eastern Naval Command: Headquartered in Visakhapatnam, it consists of the Eastern Fleet – responsible for naval operations in the Bay of Bengal, which flanks India's eastern coastline. In addition, it serves as the home command of India strategic submarine fleet – which oversees the country's nuclear second-strike deterrence force.
Southern Naval Command: Headquartered in Kochi, it is the Indian Navy's largest command – responsible for service's training requirements.
The Indian Navy's Maritime Capability Perspective Plan for the period 2012–2027 had set the objective of the service becoming a 250-ship fleet by 2035. However, as of November 2025, the service is expected to achieve a fleet size of over 200 ships by 2035. Additionally, the Indian Naval Air Arm operates more than 250 aircraft, including carrier-based aircraft, helicopters, maritime patrol aircraft, in support of the fleet.

positions.A: The Indian Navy's fleet modernization and expansion plans, though revised downward from the original 250-ship target, still represent adequate progress toward meeting India's maritime security needs.
positions.B: The reduction of the Indian Navy's projected fleet size from 250 to just over 200 ships by 2035, alongside persistent gaps like the lack of mine countermeasure vessels and insufficient attack submarines, reflects a concerning shortfall in India's naval capability planning.

title: INS Jalashwa
neutral_summary: INS Jalashwa (lit. 'Horse of the Sea') is an amphibious transport dock currently in service with the Indian Navy. Formerly USS Trenton, she, along with six Sikorsky SH-3 Sea King helicopters were procured from the United States by India for a total of US$90 million in 2005. She was commissioned on 22 June 2007. INS Jalashwa is the only Indian naval ship to be acquired from the United States. She is based in Visakhapatnam under the Eastern Naval Command.

positions.A: The acquisition of USS Trenton by India strengthened its naval capabilities and deepened strategic defense ties with the United States.
positions.B: The acquisition of USS Trenton represented an unnecessary deviation from India's traditional policy of military self-reliance and non-alignment by relying on a single US-sourced platform.

title: Vikrant-class aircraft carrier
neutral_summary:
The Vikrant class (lit. 'Courageous') (formerly Project 71 Air Defence Ship (ADS) or Indigenous Aircraft Carrier (IAC)) is a class of aircraft carrier being built for the Indian Navy. The class represents the largest warships and the first aircraft carriers to be designed and built in India.
Preparations for building the lead vessel of the class, INS Vikrant, started in 2008, and the keel was laid in February 2009. The carrier was floated out of its dry dock on 29 December 2011, launched on 12 August 2013 and commissioned on 2 September 2022. The scale and complexity of the project caused problems which delayed the construction for the carrier. Technical difficulties, the cost of refitting the Soviet-built carrier INS Vikramaditya, and billions in cost overruns delayed plans for the first of the vessels to enter service.

positions.A: The Vikrant-class program demonstrates India's growing indigenous defense capability and is a worthwhile long-term investment despite delays and cost overruns.
positions.B: The Vikrant-class program reflects poor project management and inefficiency, with excessive delays and cost overruns undermining its value to India's defense priorities.

title: Shishumar-class submarine
neutral_summary:
The Shishumar-class submarines (lit. 'Dolphin') are diesel-electric attack submarines, currently in active service with the Indian Navy. These submarines are an Indian variant of the Type 209 submarines developed by the German yard Howaldtswerke-Deutsche Werft under the internal designation "Type 1500". The first two vessels were built by HDW at Kiel, Germany, while the remainder were built by Mazagon Dock Limited, at Mumbai, India, under a technology transfer agreement. The submarines were commissioned between 1986 and 1994. These submarines have a displacement of 1,660 tons when surfaced, a speed of 22 knots (41 km/h; 25 mph), and a complement of 40 including eight officers.
The Shishumar class is unique among Type 209s for having an IKL-designed integrated escape sphere. The sphere has accommodations for the entire crew with an eight-hour air supply.
The submarines form the 10th Submarine Squadron at INS Vajrabahu, Mumbai.

positions.A: The Shishumar-class submarine deal exemplified legitimate defense modernization through technology transfer that strengthened India's indigenous submarine-building capability.
positions.B: The Shishumar-class submarine deal was marred by corruption and kickback allegations involving HDW, undermining the integrity of India's defense procurement process.

title: Sindhughosh-class submarine
neutral_summary:
Sindhughosh-class (lit. 'Roar of the Sea') submarines are Kilo-class diesel-electric submarines in active service with the Indian Navy. Their names are in Sanskrit, but in their Roman-alphabet forms sometimes a final short -a is dropped.
The Sindhughosh submarines, designated 877EKM, were designed as part of Project 877, and built under a contract between Rosvooruzhenie and the Ministry of Defence (India).
The submarines have a displacement of 3,000 tonnes, a maximum diving depth of 300 meters, top speed of 18 knots, and are able to operate solo for 45 days with a crew of 53. The final unit was the first to be equipped with the 3M-54 Klub (SS-N-27) antiship cruise missiles with a range of 220 km.
As of 2024, three of the submarines (S55, S57, S59) based at INS Vajrabahu, Mumbai, form 12th Submarine Squadron while four of the submarines (S60, S61, S62, S65) based at INS Virbahu, Mumbai, form 11th Submarine Squadron.

positions.A: The Sindhughosh-class submarines, despite their age and past accidents, remain a cost-effective and reliable backbone of India's underwater fleet through periodic upgrades.
positions.B: The Sindhughosh-class submarines are outdated Soviet-era vessels whose safety record and aging design justify accelerating their replacement with indigenous or newer platforms.

title: Kalvari-class submarine (2015)
neutral_summary:
The Kalvari-class submarines (lit. 'Tiger shark'), formally classified as the Project-75 submarines (P-75), is a class of diesel-electric attack submarines operated by the Indian Navy (IN). Built by a syndicate of French and Indian shipyards, namely, Naval Group and Mazagon Dock Limited (MDL) respectively, the class is an export derivative of the French-origin Scorpène-class submarine, originally designed by Naval Group.
A namesake of the former Foxtrot-class submarines that the IN operated between 1967 and 2010, the class was originally planned in the late-1990s as an initial phase of a 30-year long naval rearmament roadmap to replace the IN's conventional submarine fleet, namely the Sindhughosh and Shishumar-class submarines. India's Ministry of Defence (MoD) placed an order of six submarines in 2005, at a cost of ₹23,562 crore (equivalent to ₹800 billion or US$8.3 billion in 2023). The final submarine entered service on 15 January 2025. 
First introduced to operational service in 2017, the submarines are currently operated by the IN for a variety of missions, namely, littoral surveillance, intelligence gathering, anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare and minelaying operations.

positions.A: The Project-75 Kalvari-class program represents a strategic success, delivering critical submarine capabilities to the Indian Navy despite delays and enhancing India's defense self-reliance through Naval Group-MDL collaboration.
positions.B: The Project-75 Kalvari-class program reflects significant procurement failures, marked by cost overruns, years of delay, and continued dependence on foreign technology despite claims of indigenization.

title: INS Arighaat
neutral_summary:
INS Arighaat (SSBN 81) (lit. 'The one who attacks the enemy') is the second of the Indian Navy's Arihant-class submarine. It is designated S3 Strategic Strike Nuclear Submarine. The 6,000 tonne vessel was built under the Advanced Technology Vessel (ATV) project at the Ship Building Centre in the port city of Visakhapatnam.
The submarine was quietly launched in 2017 and little has been publicly announced about its capabilities and current status. The submarine was originally known as INS Aridhaman but was renamed INS Arighaat upon its launch. Arighaat was commissioned on 29 August 2024.

positions.A: INS Arighaat strengthens India's credible nuclear deterrence and completes its nuclear triad, enhancing national security.
positions.B: The development of INS Arighaat escalates regional nuclear competition and raises tensions with neighboring states like China and Pakistan.

title: INS Arihant
neutral_summary: INS Arihant (SSBN 80) (lit. 'Conqueror'), is the lead ship of Indian Navy's Arihant class of nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines. The vessel was built under the Advanced Technology Vessel project at the Ship Building Centre in Visakhapatnam. The submarine was launched on 26 July 2009, and after fitting out and extensive sea trials, she was commissioned in August 2016, and deployed operationally in 2018.

positions.A: INS Arihant is a necessary and stabilizing addition to India's nuclear deterrent, completing its credible second-strike capability under a no-first-use doctrine.
positions.B: INS Arihant escalates regional nuclear competition and increases strategic instability in South Asia by prompting countermeasures from rival states.

title: 2026 Iran war fuel crisis
neutral_summary:
The 2026 Iran war fuel crisis is a worldwide fuel crisis caused by the war between Iran and the U.S.-Israel coalition. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which over 20% of the world's oil trade passes, and attacks on energy infrastructure in Iran and several Gulf Cooperation Council countries led to a large disruption in global oil supplies. The disruption led to global oil prices rising and caused fuel shortages in countries which imported most of their fuel from the Persian Gulf region. Much of the world has been affected by panic buying and severe disruption to the distribution of petroleum products, liquefied natural gas (LNG), and urea used for fertiliser. 
The economies of most countries are expected to be adversely affected by the crisis, leading to inflation and heightened risks of stagflation and recession. As of April 2026 there was ongoing concerns about energy security as well as food security, related to fertiliser shortages and costs.
By July 2026, brent prices fell from a peak of $118.35 in March 31, 2026 to $71.57 in July 01, 2026, but increased to $96.78 by July 24.By June 2026, the yearly inflation rate is 3.53%, with the consumer price index decreasing by 0.42% and weekly earnings increasing by 0.77% since May 2026. On July, the IMF revised its world GDP growth rate to 3% for 2026 and 3.4% in 2027.According to IMF the effect of the oil supply shock on the world economy is limited due to the AI-driven demand.

positions.A: The fuel crisis is primarily the result of Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on regional energy infrastructure, making Iran responsible for the global economic damage.
positions.B: The fuel crisis is primarily the result of the U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran, which provoked the disruption of oil flows and should bear responsibility for the global economic damage.

title: Gokha (caste)
neutral_summary: Gokha, also known as Gakha are a fishing community found in Odisha and are concentrated in the coastal districts of the state, particularly in the Balasore and its adjacing districts. They are recognized as Scheduled Castes in the state of Odisha, with a population of 2,12,718 as per 2011 census of India.

positions.A: The Gokha community's classification as a Scheduled Caste accurately reflects their historical socio-economic marginalization and warrants the reservation benefits they currently receive.
positions.B: The Gokha community should be reclassified under a different category (such as Scheduled Tribe or Other Backward Class) because their current Scheduled Caste status does not adequately address their distinct social and economic circumstances.

title: 2026 attack on Israeli consulate in Istanbul
neutral_summary: On 7 April, 2026, three gunmen attacked the Israeli Consulate in Istanbul, Turkey. One attacker was killed while two other gunmen and two police officers sustained injuries. Both Turkey and Israel declared the attack an act of terrorism.

positions.A: The attack on the Israeli consulate was an act of terrorism that Turkey and Israel are right to jointly condemn and prosecute.
positions.B: The attack should be understood as a violent expression of protest against Israeli policy in Gaza rather than simply being labeled terrorism.

title: List of battles involving the Mughal Empire
neutral_summary: The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526 by Babur. He defeated Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat, marking the beginning of Mughal dominance. Babur went on to defeat the powerful Rajput confederacy of Rana Sanga in his decisive victory in the Battle of Khanwa, which solidified Mughal rule in India. The empire continued to expand, reaching its greatest territorial extent during the reign of Aurangzeb.

positions.A: The Mughal Empire's military conquests, such as those at Panipat and Khanwa, represent a violent foreign invasion that subjugated indigenous Indian kingdoms like the Rajputs.
positions.B: The Mughal Empire's military campaigns were legitimate state-building efforts that unified diverse regions of India under a stable and culturally rich administration.

title: Isa Khan
neutral_summary: Isa Khan (Middle Bengali: ঈশা খাঁ, 17 April 1536 – 29 August 1599) was one of the 16th-century Baro-Bhuyan chieftains of Bengal. During his reign, he successfully unified the chieftains of Bengal and resisted the Mughal invasion of Bengal. It was only after his death that the region fell totally under Mughal control. He remains an iconic figure throughout Bangladesh as a symbol of his rebellious spirit and unity.

positions.A: Isa Khan should be remembered as a heroic unifier who successfully resisted Mughal expansion and preserved regional autonomy for the Baro-Bhuyan chieftains.
positions.B: Isa Khan's resistance was ultimately a futile delay of inevitable and legitimate Mughal consolidation of Bengal, which brought administrative unity to the region.

title: Outline of the 2026 Iran war
neutral_summary: The following outline is provided as an overview of and topical guide to the Wikipedia articles available about the 2026 Iran war. It is an evolving list.

positions.A: The 2026 military action against Iran was a necessary and justified response to counter an imminent threat, such as nuclear proliferation or regional aggression.
positions.B: The 2026 military action against Iran was an unjustified act of aggression that violated international law and destabilized the region.

title: Agni (missile)
neutral_summary: The Agni missile (Sanskrit: अग्नि; lit. Fire) is a family of medium to intercontinental range ballistic missiles developed by India, named after one of the five elements of nature. Agni missiles are long-range, nuclear weapons capable, surface-to-surface ballistic missiles. The first missile of the series, Agni-I was developed under the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (lGMDP) and tested in 1989. After its success, the Agni missile programme was separated from the GMDP upon realizing its strategic importance. It was designated as a special programme in India's defence budget and provided adequate funds for subsequent development.

positions.A: The Agni missile programme is a necessary and legitimate component of India's strategic deterrence, ensuring national security against regional nuclear-armed rivals.
positions.B: The Agni missile programme escalates regional arms races and nuclear proliferation risks, destabilizing security dynamics in South Asia and beyond.

title: Surya missile
neutral_summary: The Surya missile (lit. 'Sun') is a speculated intercontinental ballistic missile being developed by Defence research and development organization of India. Its operational range is beyond 18,000 Km, covering the entire earth.

positions.A: The Surya missile program represents a legitimate and necessary step for India to develop credible intercontinental deterrence capability amid regional security challenges.
positions.B: The Surya missile program is a destabilizing development that risks fueling a regional arms race and undermining global non-proliferation efforts.

title: Agni-VI
neutral_summary: Agni-VI (Sanskrit: अग्नि; IAST: Agni; lit. Fire) is an MIRV-capable intercontinental ballistic missile under development by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) for the Strategic Forces Command (SFC) of the Indian Armed Forces.

positions.A: Agni-VI is a necessary strategic deterrent that strengthens India's security by countering regional nuclear threats and maintaining credible minimum deterrence.
positions.B: Agni-VI escalates a regional arms race and increases nuclear proliferation risks in South Asia, undermining stability rather than enhancing security.

title: Agni-IV
neutral_summary: Agni-IV (lit. 'Fire') is the fourth in the Agni series of missiles which was earlier known as Agni II prime. It has been developed by India's DRDO and displayed a number of new technologies and significant improvement in missile technology. The missile is light-weight and has two stages of solid propulsion and a payload with re-entry heat shield. With 4,000 km range, it is capable of striking targets in nearly all of mainland China, if launched from northeastern part of India.

positions.A: Agni-IV is a necessary strategic deterrent that strengthens India's defense capability against regional threats, particularly China.
positions.B: Agni-IV's development and range escalate regional tensions and contribute to a destabilizing arms race in South Asia.

title: Agni-III
neutral_summary: The Agni-III (lit. 'Fire') is an Indian intermediate-range ballistic missile inducted into service in 2011 as the successor of the Agni-II. It has a range of 3,500 kilometres (2,200 mi) and can reach targets deep inside neighbouring countries including Pakistan and China.

positions.A: The Agni-III is a necessary strategic deterrent that ensures India's security against regional nuclear-armed threats from China and Pakistan.
positions.B: The Agni-III contributes to a dangerous regional arms race and escalates nuclear tensions in South Asia.

title: Agni-II
neutral_summary:
Agni-II (lit. 'Fire'), is the second strategic ballistic missile of the Agni family envisaged to be the mainstay of the Indian missile-based strategic nuclear deterrence. The Agni-II is a medium-range ballistic missile (MRBM) with two solid fuel stages and a Post Boost Vehicle (PBV) integrated into the missile's Re-entry Vehicle (RV). The Agni's manoeuvring RV is made of a carbon-carbon composite material that is light and able to sustain high thermal stresses of re-entry, in a variety of trajectories. The Agni-IIA is a more advanced version of Agni-II, albeit with more sophisticated and lighter materials, yielding a better range and operating regime. Agni-IIA was later renamed as Agni-IV plugging the gap between Agni-II and Agni-III. While the first test of Agni-IV in December 2010 was a failure, the second test flight in November 2011 was a success Agni-II, developed as part of medium- and long-range Agni series of missile systems, has already been inducted into the Armed Forces.

On 17 May 2010, the trial was conducted with a Strategic Forces Command (SFC) of nuclear-capable Agni-II ballistic missile, with a range of 2,000 kilometres from the Wheelers Island off Orissa coast thus making Agni-II missile operational by army. US Air Force National Air and Space Intelligence Center estimating that as of June 2017 less than 10 launchers were operationally deployed, operated by the 335 Missile Group of Regiment of Artillery at Secunderabad using 12 TEL vehicles.
Agni-II can reach all of Pakistan and most parts of south and southeastern China.

positions.A: Agni-II is a necessary and stabilizing component of India's nuclear deterrence, justified by security threats from Pakistan and China.
positions.B: Agni-II's development and deployment fuels a destabilizing regional arms race and increases nuclear proliferation risks in South Asia.

title: Agni-P
neutral_summary: Agni-Prime or Agni-P (Sanskrit: अग्नि; IAST: Agni; lit. Fire) is a two-stage, surface to surface, canister-launched, road mobile and solid-fueled medium-range ballistic missile being developed by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) as the sixth missile in the Agni series. It is intended to be deployed in the operational service of the Strategic Forces Command, and to feature significant upgrades to the composite motor casing, a maneuverable reentry vehicle (MaRV) along with improved propellants, navigation and guidance systems.

positions.A: India's development of the Agni-P missile is a necessary and stabilizing step for national security, deterrence, and strategic autonomy in a challenging regional environment.
positions.B: India's development of the Agni-P missile risks fueling a regional arms race and heightening nuclear tensions in South Asia.

title: Shaurya (missile)
neutral_summary: Shaurya (lit. 'Valour') is a hypersonic, canister-launched surface-to-surface short-range ballistic missile developed by the Indian Defence Research and Development Organisation for use by the Indian Armed Forces. It has a range of 700 to 1,900 km (430 to 1,180 mi) and is capable of carrying a payload of 200 to 1,000 kg (440 to 2,200 lb) conventional or nuclear warhead.

positions.A: The Shaurya missile is a necessary strategic asset that strengthens India's credible nuclear deterrent and regional security posture.
positions.B: The Shaurya missile's development and deployment fuels a destabilizing arms race and heightens nuclear risk in South Asia.

title: Agni-I
neutral_summary: Agni-I (lit. 'Fire') is a short-range ballistic missile that was developed by DRDO of India in the Integrated Guided Missile Development Program. It is a single-stage missile that was developed after the Kargil War to fill the gap between the 250 km (160-mile) range of the Prithvi-II missile and the 2,500 km (1,600-mile) range of the Agni-II. It was first launched from a road mobile launcher at Integrated Test Range (ITR), Wheeler Island, on 25 January 2002. Less than 75 launchers are deployed.

positions.A: Agni-I is a necessary strategic deterrent that fills a critical gap in India's missile capability against regional threats.
positions.B: Agni-I's development and deployment contributes to a destabilizing arms race and heightens nuclear tensions in South Asia.

title: Abu Maher Ghneim
neutral_summary: Muhammad "Abu Maher" Ghneim (Arabic: محمد "أبو ماهر" راتب غنيم; born 1937) is a Palestinian politician and a senior Fatah official, being a member of the organization's central committee.

positions.A: Abu Maher Ghneim represents the legitimate nationalist leadership of Fatah advocating for Palestinian statehood through political and diplomatic means.
positions.B: Abu Maher Ghneim, as part of the Fatah old guard, is viewed by critics as emblematic of an entrenched leadership resistant to reform and accountability.

title: SMART (missile)
neutral_summary: SMART (Supersonic Missile Assisted Release of Torpedo) is a canister-based, long-range supersonic anti-submarine missile developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) for the Indian Navy.

positions.A: The SMART missile system enhances India's strategic deterrence and anti-submarine warfare capabilities in a way that promotes regional stability.
positions.B: The SMART missile system escalates the regional arms race and heightens military tensions in South Asia.

title: Mission Sudarshan Chakra
neutral_summary:
Mission Sudarshan Chakra is an Indian defence initiative to develop an interlocked, multi-layered, all-encompassing, AI-enabled networked architecture that combines enhanced monitoring, cyber protection, and physical defense to protect Indian population and infrastructure against terrorist attacks, military strikes, and other high value threats. The idea behind the defense barrier is similar to the Iron Dome of Israel and the Golden Dome of the United States. The Defence Research and Development Organisation is the main entity spearheading the project.
The programme's goal is to establish a national multi-domain offensive and defensive security umbrella. It is to facilitate quick, accurate, and effective defense response against multi-vector threats such as ballistic missiles, hypersonic platforms, fighter aircraft, loitering munitions, swarm drones etc.

positions.A: Mission Sudarshan Chakra is a necessary and forward-looking defense initiative that will protect India's population and infrastructure from evolving multi-domain threats like missiles, drones, and cyberattacks.
positions.B: Mission Sudarshan Chakra is an overly ambitious and costly project that risks escalating regional tensions and diverting resources without guaranteed technological feasibility.

title: Defence Space Agency
neutral_summary:
The Defence Space Agency (DSA) is an integrated tri-services agency of the Indian Armed Forces headquartered in Bengaluru, Karnataka. The agency is tasked with operating the space warfare and satellite intelligence assets of India. The DSA draws personnel from all three branches of the Armed Forces.
The agency is expected to be converted into a full sized tri-service military command in the future.

positions.A: India needs a dedicated tri-service Defence Space Agency to protect its strategic and security interests in an increasingly contested space domain.
positions.B: Establishing a dedicated space warfare agency risks accelerating the militarization of space and diverting resources from other pressing defense priorities.

title: List of Indian military missiles
neutral_summary: The Indian Armed Forces uses various types of ballistic and cruise missiles. In India, the Defence Research and Development Organisation is the major body that is involved in the research and development of missiles. Public sector units and some of the private organizations are involved in the manufacture of the missiles, often in collaboration with foreign manufacturers. India also procures missiles from foreign manufacturers and agencies.

positions.A: India's continued indigenous development and expansion of its ballistic and cruise missile arsenal, including nuclear-capable systems, is a necessary and legitimate measure for national defense and strategic deterrence.
positions.B: India's rapid expansion and diversification of its missile arsenal, including nuclear-capable systems, fuels a destabilizing regional arms race and heightens security risks in South Asia.

title: Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme
neutral_summary:
The Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) was an Indian Ministry of Defence programme for the research and development of the comprehensive range of missiles. The programme was managed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Ordnance Factories Board in partnership with other Indian government political organisations. The project started in 1982–83 under the leadership of Abdul Kalam who oversaw its ending in 2008 after these strategic missiles were successfully developed.
On 8 January 2008, the DRDO formally announced the successful rated guided missile programme was completed with its design objectives achieved since most of the missiles in the programme had been developed and inducted by the Indian Armed Forces.

positions.A: The IGMDP was a necessary and successful indigenous initiative that gave India strategic autonomy and credible deterrence capability.
positions.B: The IGMDP contributed to regional arms escalation and diverted significant resources toward militarization rather than other national priorities.

title: Indian Army
neutral_summary:
The Indian Army (IA) (ISO: Bhāratīya Sēnā) is the land-based branch and largest component of the Indian Armed Forces. The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the Indian Army, and its professional head is the Chief of the Army Staff (COAS). The Indian Army was established on 1 April 1895 alongside the long established presidency armies of the East India Company, which too were absorbed into it in 1903. Some princely states maintained their own armies which formed the Imperial Service Troops which, along with the Indian Army formed the land component of the Armed Forces of the Crown of India, responsible for the defence of the Indian Empire. The Imperial Service Troops were merged into the Indian Army after independence. The units and regiments of the Indian Army have diverse histories and have participated in several battles and campaigns around the world, earning many battle and theatre honours before and after Independence.
The primary mission of the Indian Army is to ensure national security and national unity, to defend the nation from external aggression and internal threats, and to maintain peace and security within its borders. It conducts humanitarian rescue operations during natural calamities and other disturbances, such as Operation Surya Hope, and can also be requisitioned by the government to cope with internal threats. It is a major component of national power, alongside the Indian Navy and the Indian Air Force. The independent Indian army has been involved in four wars with neighbouring Pakistan and one with China. It has emerged victorious in all wars against Pakistan. Other major operations undertaken by the army include Operation Vijay, Operation Meghdoot, and Operation Cactus. The army has conducted large peacetime exercises such as Operation Brasstacks and Exercise Shoorveer, and it has also been an active participant in numerous United Nations peacekeeping missions. The Indian Army was a major force in the First and Second World Wars, particularly in the Western Front and the Middle Eastern theatre during World War I, and the South-East Asian Theatre and the East African and North African campaigns during World War II.
The Indian Army is operationally and geographically divided into seven commands, with the basic field formation being a division. The army is an all-volunteer force and comprises more than 80% of the country's active defence personnel. It is the largest standing army in the world, with 1,248,000 active troops and 960,000 reserve troops. The army has embarked on an infantry modernisation program known as Futuristic Infantry Soldier As a System (F-INSAS), and is also upgrading and acquiring new assets for its armoured, artillery, and aviation branches.

positions.A: The Indian Army acts as a legitimate national defense force that has successfully protected India's sovereignty and territorial integrity in conflicts with Pakistan and China.
positions.B: The Indian Army's operations, particularly in contested regions like Kashmir, have involved human rights abuses and excessive use of force against civilian populations.

title: Indian Naval Ensign
neutral_summary: The Indian Naval Ensign, also referred to as the Indian White Ensign, or Nishaan, is the naval ensign of the Indian Navy (IN), used aboard Indian naval vessels, shore establishments and naval air stations as its principal form of maritime identification.

positions.A: The Indian Naval Ensign should remove colonial-era symbols like the St George's Cross to reflect India's postcolonial national identity.
positions.B: The Indian Naval Ensign should retain traditional naval symbols such as the St George's Cross as part of India's historical naval heritage.

title: HMIS Talwar
neutral_summary: HMIS (His Majesty's Indian Ship) Talwar was a shore establishment of the British Royal Indian Navy during World War II in Colaba, Bombay.

positions.A: The 1946 mutiny centered at HMIS Talwar was a significant and courageous catalyst that accelerated the British decision to leave India.
positions.B: The events at HMIS Talwar were primarily a disciplinary breakdown among naval ratings with limited real impact on the timing of British withdrawal from India.

title: Royal Indian Navy
neutral_summary:
The Royal Indian Navy (RIN) was the naval force of the erstwhile British Raj and its successor Dominion of India. Along with the presidency armies, later the Indian Army, and from 1932 the Royal Indian Air Force, it was one of the Armed Forces of British India.
From its origins in 1612 as the East India Company's Marine, the Navy underwent various changes, including changes to its name. Over time it was named the Bombay Marine (1686), the Bombay Marine Corps (1829), the Indian Navy (1830), Her Majesty's Indian Navy (1858), the Bombay and Bengal Marine (1863), the Indian Defence Force (1871), Her Majesty's Indian Marine (1877) and the Royal Indian Marine (1892). It was finally named the Royal Indian Navy in 1934. However, it remained a relatively small force until the Second World War, when it was greatly expanded.
After the partition of India into two independent states in 1947, the Navy was split between India and Pakistan.  One-third of the assets and personnel were assigned to the Pakistan Navy. Approximately two thirds of the fleet remained with the Union of India, as did all land assets within its territory.   This force, still under the name of "Royal Indian Navy", became the navy of the Dominion of India until the country became a republic on 26 January 1950. It was then renamed the Indian Navy.

positions.A: The division of Royal Indian Navy assets in 1947, with Pakistan receiving only one-third of ships and personnel, was a fair reflection of the relative populations and needs of the two new dominions.
positions.B: The 1947 division of Royal Indian Navy assets was inequitable, leaving Pakistan with a disproportionately small and inadequate naval inheritance compared to India.

title: Muhammad Youssef al-Najjar
neutral_summary: Muhammad Youssef Al-Najjar (Arabic: محمد يوسف النجار; 11 June 1930 – 10 April 1973), commonly known as Abu Youssef, was a Palestinian militant who was assassinated by Israeli commandos over alleged involvement in the 1972 Munich massacre.

positions.A: The assassination of Muhammad Youssef al-Najjar was a legitimate act of counter-terrorism justified by his alleged role in the Munich massacre.
positions.B: The assassination of Muhammad Youssef al-Najjar was an extrajudicial killing that violated international law and due process.

title: Na'ale
neutral_summary:
Na'ale (Hebrew: נעלה, lit. 'Exalted') is an Israeli settlement in the West Bank. Located near Modi'in, it falls under the jurisdiction of Mateh Binyamin Regional Council. In 2024 it had a population of 2,932.
The international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, but the Israeli government disputes this.
The settlement was built on land confiscated from the Palestinian towns of Al-Ittihad (Jammala), Deir Qaddis and Shabtin.

positions.A: Na'ale is an illegal settlement built on confiscated Palestinian land in violation of international law.
positions.B: Na'ale is a legitimate Israeli settlement whose establishment does not violate international law, a position maintained by the Israeli government.

title: Shvut Rachel
neutral_summary: Shvut Rachel (Hebrew: שבות רחל) is a former Israeli settlement in the West Bank, retroactively designated a neighborhood of the settlement of Shilo, in the West Bank. Shvut Rachel sits between the Palestinian villages of Turmus Ayya, Qaryut and Jalud, part of whose lands were expropriated for building Shvut Rachel. Nearby Israeli settlements include Shilo, Giv'at Har'el, Esh Kodesh, Keeda, and Adei Ad. The village, administrated by the Matte Binyamin Regional Council, has a population of 100 families. The international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, but the Israeli government disputes this. The Sasson Report in 2005 noted that the settlement extends over Palestinian land, part of which is owned by Fawzi Haj Ibrahim Mohammad from Jalud, turned over to the settlement after the Israeli authorities declared it state land.

positions.A: Shvut Rachel is an illegal settlement built on expropriated Palestinian land in violation of international law.
positions.B: Shvut Rachel is a legitimate Israeli community established on land legally designated by Israeli authorities, and its status is an internal matter not bound by international law as Israel interprets it.

title: Sasson Report
neutral_summary: The Sasson Report is an official Israeli government report published on 8 March 2005 that concluded that Israeli state bodies had been discreetly diverting millions of shekels to build West Bank settlements and outposts that were illegal under Israeli law. The report was commissioned by the Prime Minister Ariel Sharon, and was headed by the former head of the State Prosecution Criminal Department Talia Sasson. Talia Sasson would later run for the Israeli elections as part of the left wing party Meretz.

positions.A: The Sasson Report exposed a genuine and serious abuse of state funds by Israeli officials to illegally finance settlements and outposts, and its findings should prompt accountability and enforcement of the law.
positions.B: The Sasson Report was a politically motivated attempt by the Sharon government and its allies to delegitimize and undermine the settlement movement, exaggerating minor bureaucratic irregularities into a scandal.

title: Nofei Nehemia
neutral_summary:
Nofei Nehemia (Hebrew: נוֹפֵי נְחֶמְיָה) is an Israeli outpost in the West Bank, in the jurisdiction of the Shomron Regional Council in the northern West Bank. It is officially within the boundaries of Rehelim, a nearby Israeli settlement. First established in 2002, it is situated adjacent to Rechelim on Route 60, between Kfar Tapuach and Eli. The village also lies adjacent to the Palestinian towns of Iskaka and Yasuf. A few dozen families live on the village.
Israeli outposts are illegal under international law and also under Israeli law.

positions.A: Nofei Nehemia is an illegitimate outpost that violates both international law and Israeli law, and should be dismantled.
positions.B: Nofei Nehemia is a legitimate Jewish community in the historic Land of Israel that should be allowed to remain and be formally recognized.

title: Sha'ar Binyamin Industrial Zone
neutral_summary:
Sha'ar Binyamin (Hebrew: שער בנימין) is an Israeli light industrial park in the occupied West Bank, built in 1998 over land expropriated from the Palestinian villages of  Jaba' and Mukhmas. It is located in the Mateh Binyamin Regional Council, Israeli-occupied West Bank, located 2km north of Geva Binyamin on Route 60 and about 5 minutes drive from Pisgat Ze'ev in Jerusalem. The park covers an area of 606 dunams (150 acres).
The international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, but the Israeli government disputes this.

positions.A: Sha'ar Binyamin Industrial Zone is an illegal settlement built on expropriated Palestinian land from Jaba' and Mukhmas, violating international law and Palestinian property rights.
positions.B: Sha'ar Binyamin Industrial Zone is a legitimate Israeli development project in an area under Israeli administration, and Israel disputes that it violates international law.

title: Destruction of cultural heritage sites during the 2026 Iran War
neutral_summary: During the 2026 Iran war, various cultural heritage sites across West Asia were damaged or destroyed.

positions.A: The military actions that damaged or destroyed cultural heritage sites were a foreseeable and unjustifiable consequence of the warring parties' operations, warranting condemnation as violations of cultural protection norms.
positions.B: The damage to cultural heritage sites was an unintended and unavoidable byproduct of legitimate military operations, and responsibility should not be attributed as a deliberate violation of cultural protection norms.

title: Başbağlar massacre
neutral_summary: The Başbağlar massacre (Turkish: Başbağlar Katliamı) is the name given to the 5 July 1993 massacre of 33 civilians in the village of Başbağlar (which was then burnt down), in Erzincan Province during the Kurdish-Turkish conflict. While the attack was originally attributed to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), the former Turkish special forces soldier Ayhan Çarkın claimed that the deep state was behind the massacre. But later he then said that all of his claims were "just predictions". The leader of the PKK, Abdullah Öcalan while in prison stated that massacre was committed by a PKK member codenamed "Dr. Baran".

positions.A: The Başbağlar massacre was carried out by the PKK as part of its campaign against civilians during the Kurdish-Turkish conflict.
positions.B: The Başbağlar massacre was orchestrated or facilitated by elements of the Turkish deep state rather than being a genuine PKK operation.

title: Yavi massacre
neutral_summary: Yavi massacre was a mass shooting organized by the PKK on October 25, 1993 in the Yavi neighbourhood of Çat district of Erzurum, Turkey.

positions.A: The PKK carried out the Yavi massacre as a deliberate attack on civilians in the context of its armed campaign against the Turkish state.
positions.B: The PKK denies or disputes responsibility for the Yavi massacre, framing the incident differently from the official Turkish account.

title: R. C. Majumdar
neutral_summary: Ramesh Chandra Majumdar (known as R. C. Majumdar; 4 December 1884 – 11 February 1980) was an Indian historian and professor, who principally studied the history of India. He is regarded as belonging to the Hindu nationalist school of Indian historiography.

positions.A: R. C. Majumdar's historiography represents rigorous, source-based scholarship on Indian history that corrected colonial and Marxist distortions.
positions.B: R. C. Majumdar's historiography reflects a Hindu nationalist bias that shaped his interpretation of Indian history, particularly regarding Muslim rule and Indian nationalism.

title: Sha'arei Tikva
neutral_summary:
Sha'arei Tikva (Hebrew: שַׁעֲרֵי תִּקְוָה, lit. 'Gates of Hope') is an Israeli settlement in the West Bank at an elevation of 200 metres. Located northeast of Rosh HaAyin and one kilometre east of the Green Line near Elkana, it is organised as a community settlement and falls under the jurisdiction of Shomron Regional Council. In 2021 it had a population of 6,122.
The international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, but the Israeli government disputes this.

positions.A: Sha'arei Tikva and other Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law because they violate the Fourth Geneva Convention's prohibition on transferring civilians into occupied territory.
positions.B: Sha'arei Tikva is a legitimate Israeli community, and the Israeli government disputes that its presence in the West Bank violates international law.

title: Jashodaben Modi
neutral_summary: Jashodaben Narendrabhai Modi (née Chimanlal Modi; born 1952) is an Indian former school teacher and the estranged wife of Narendra Modi, the Prime Minister of India. The couple were married in 1968 when she was 16–17 and Modi was 18. About two years into the marriage, her husband, Narendra Modi, abandoned her. He did not acknowledge the marriage publicly until he was legally required to do so prior to the 2014 Indian general elections. In 2015, Jashodaben retired from her teaching job.

positions.A: Narendra Modi's long concealment of his marriage and abandonment of Jashodaben reflects a personal betrayal and dishonesty that is relevant to his public integrity.
positions.B: Narendra Modi's marital status was a private matter that he was entitled to keep out of public and political discourse until legally required to disclose it.

title: Al Jahra Force
neutral_summary:
The Al Jahra Force was a Kuwait task force, of roughly brigade strength, requested by then, Kuwait Minister of Defense, Sheikh Saad Al-Salim Al-Sabah and formed by Major General Mubarak Abdullah Al-Jaber Al-Sabah and his deputy Brigadier General Saleh Mohammed Al-Sabah; subsequently being tasked to the respective combat commanders on October 15, 1973, after the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War. The force, consisting of more than 3,000 men, was organized into a Tank Battalion, an infantry battalion, two companies of artillery, an anti-aircraft company and a combat company of the Kuwait 25th Commando Brigade. In addition, the task force also included medical, engineering and signal units. The brigade remained active until the end of September 1974, and then returned to Kuwait after a farewell ceremony in Damascus.
The task force was equipped with Vickers main battle tanks, Ferret armoured car, and Alvis Saracen. The first combat company equipped artillery batteries type Mk F3 155mm self-propelled guns  while the second combat company packed 120 mm mortars type. The anti-tank combat units were equipped with Carl Gustav recoilless rifle. The anti-aircraft combat company was equipped with triple barrel anti-aircraft guns type 20 mm, Zastava M55.

positions.A: Kuwait's deployment of the Al Jahra Force to the Syrian front demonstrated meaningful Arab solidarity and a genuine military contribution to the 1973 war effort.
positions.B: Kuwait's deployment of the Al Jahra Force was a largely symbolic gesture that saw limited direct combat involvement compared to the frontline Arab states.

title: House of Holkar
neutral_summary:
The Holkars (pronunciation: [ɦo(ː)ɭkəɾ]) were the ruling house of the Indore State of the Maratha Confederacy, and earlier held the rank of Subahdar under Peshwa Baji Rao I of the Maratha Empire. When the Maratha Confederacy began to weaken due to internal clashes, the Holkars declared themselves the rulers of Indore in Central India, existing as an autonomous member of the Maratha Confederacy until 1818. Later, their kingdom became a princely state under the British protection.
Usha Devi Holkar, 15th Maharani of Indore, is the current titular head.

positions.A: The Holkars were legitimate sovereign rulers who established an autonomous, self-governing state within the Maratha Confederacy.
positions.B: The Holkars remained subordinate vassals, first under the Peshwa's authority and later under British paramountcy, without true sovereign independence.

title: Revolutionary Palestinian Communist Party
neutral_summary:
The Revolutionary Palestinian Communist Party (Arabic: الحزب الشيوعي الفلسطيني-الثوري) is a small Palestinian political party, founded in October 1982. Arabi Awwad was the general secretary of the party. As of the early 2000s, the party headquarters were in Damascus. The party calls for the establishment  of an independent Palestinian state on "all national soil" through armed struggle.
The RPCP emerged from a split in the West Bank branch of the Jordanian Communist Party in 1982, over the issue of recognizing the State of Israel. The moderates formed the Palestinian Communist Party, which adhered to the Soviet line of recognizing Israel. The radical group, led by former West Bank party secretary Awwad, formed the Revolutionary Palestinian Communist Party. The RPCP joined the PLO. The party supported the Palestinian National Alliance, but did not formally join it. Apart from Awwad, other politburo members of the party included Jiryis Qawwas and Abdullah Nimr.
The RPCP took part in the armed resistance against the Israeli invasion in Lebanon; a number of party members (including Awwad's son Fahd Awwad) were killed during this struggle.
The RPCP broke away from the PLO in 1987, in rejection of what they saw as rapprochement by Yasser Arafat with imperialist forces (notably, the Palestinian Communist Party joined the PLO just afterwards). The party vehemently opposed the Oslo Accords. In the early 1990s, the RPCP disbanded its armed wing (after a long period of inactivity). In 1994 the RPCP joined the Alliance of Palestinian Forces.
The party argues that the armed Syrian opposition is supported by colonialist, Zionist and reactionary forces.  These are said to be seeking to weaken the Arab states in order to dominate the region. Awwad died in March 2015.

positions.A: Achieving Palestinian statehood requires armed struggle to liberate all historic Palestinian land and rejecting compromises like recognition of Israel or the Oslo Accords.
positions.B: Palestinian national goals are better pursued through diplomatic recognition of Israel and negotiated agreements such as the Oslo Accords rather than continued armed struggle.

title: Southern Army (Syria)
neutral_summary: The Southern Army (Arabic: "جيش الجنوب") was an Israeli-proposed paramilitary force in southern Syria, aimed at establishing an Israeli friendly force at a buffer zone along the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights and to deter Iranian and Hezbollah influence in the region.

positions.A: The Southern Army was a legitimate Israeli-backed initiative to create a stabilizing buffer force that would protect Israel's border and counter Iranian and Hezbollah expansion in southern Syria.
positions.B: The Southern Army was an illegitimate foreign-engineered proxy force that violated Syrian sovereignty by attempting to install Israeli-aligned militias inside Syrian territory.

title: Sinai Mujahideen
neutral_summary: The Sinai Mujahideen were a militant group during the War of Attrition between Egypt and Israel.  It was initially organized when Egyptian military intelligence reached out to Eid Abu Jarir, who was asked to recruit seven fellow tribal members, and helped start three branches based in Port Said, Ismailia and Suez. Besides Jarir, it drew strength from other Bedouin Sufi Darqawa figures such as Khalaf al-Khalafat, as well as its most important military leader, Hassan Khalaf. In 1997, A veterans group under this name is currently organized under the Egyptian NGO Law, which has also been active in opposing Ansar Bait al-Maqdis.

positions.A: The Sinai Mujahideen were a genuine grassroots Bedouin resistance movement that organized to fight Israeli occupation during the War of Attrition.
positions.B: The Sinai Mujahideen were essentially a proxy force created and directed by Egyptian military intelligence rather than an independent resistance movement.

title: 69 Squadron (Israel)
neutral_summary:
The 69 "Hammers" Squadron is an Israeli Air Force squadron operating the F-15I Thunder out of Hatzerim. It was formed in July 1948 to operate three B-17 Flying Fortresses which the fledgling Israeli Air Force had acquired in the United States. The squadron flew the Flying Fortress, an aircraft credited with propelling the IAF into the realm of modern aerial warfare, during both the 1948 Arab–Israeli War and 1956 Suez Crisis. Disbanded in early 1957, 69 Squadron reformed in 1969 to fly the F-4 Phantom II. 
69 Squadron operated the Kurnass (Sledgehammer), as the Phantom was known in Israel, for 25 years. Its Phantoms saw extensive action during the War of Attrition, Yom Kippur War, First Lebanon War and numerous engagements in between. The squadron often played a central role in IAF suppression of enemy air defences (SEAD) efforts and took part in repeated battles against Egyptian and Syrian air defence.
The squadron retired its Phantoms in 1994 and reformed shortly thereafter to operate the F-15I Thunder. Described as the "long-range, heavy bombing element of Israeli air power", 69 Squadron, together with Squadrons 119 and 253, carried out Operation Outside the Box, the September 2007 airstrike on a nuclear site in Syria.

positions.A: The 2007 airstrike on the Syrian site (Operation Outside the Box) was a legitimate and necessary act of self-defense to prevent a hostile state from acquiring nuclear weapons capability.
positions.B: The 2007 airstrike on the Syrian site (Operation Outside the Box) was an unlawful violation of Syrian sovereignty that set a dangerous precedent for unilateral military action.

title: Reagan peace plan
neutral_summary: The Reagan peace plan, also known as the Reagan Middle East peace plan, was announced by United States President Ronald Reagan during a speech on September 1, 1982. The plan's stated goals was to "reconcile Israel's legitimate security concerns with the legitimate rights of the Palestinians." It proposed a five-year transition period, during which Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza would obtain full autonomy, and an association of the territories with Jordan.

positions.A: The Reagan plan offered a reasonable framework for Palestinian self-governance through autonomy and association with Jordan, without destabilizing the region via full statehood.
positions.B: The Reagan plan was inadequate because it denied Palestinians full national sovereignty and self-determination by ruling out an independent Palestinian state.

title: Quartet Principles
neutral_summary:
The Quartet Principles are the set of three requirements laid out by the Quartet on the Middle East for the diplomatic recognition of a Palestinian government as part of the Israeli–Palestinian peace process. The three conditions are: 1) non-violence, 2) recognition of the state of Israel, and 3) to respect previous Israel-Palestinian peace agreements.
The principles were first outlined on in October 2005 and reaffirmed in January 2006, after Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative election. Hamas did not accept the conditions set out in the principles.

positions.A: The Quartet Principles are a reasonable and necessary precondition for legitimizing any Palestinian government, ensuring commitment to peaceful negotiation and prior agreements.
